attempts.label: CRCNS:hc-30
attempts.entry_title: Noise correlations limit hippocampal spatial accuracy (Hazon et al. 2022)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings held up: noise correlations among CA1 place cells were strongest for nearby place fields, worsened position decoding, made accuracy saturate with ensemble size, and cost most in mice with a low normalized signal variance. Two details differ: the signal-to-noise ratio along noise components peaked at the 7th component, not the 6th, and the signal slope rose over runs, opposite to the Figure 3f legend. The ensemble size at which accuracy saturates did not reproduce, possibly owing to this attempt's decoder. Whether correlations depend on the distance between cells could not be tested, as the dataset lacks cell positions. Supplementary place-field statistics and the link between task performance and accuracy did not reproduce.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Hazon, Minces, Tomàs, Ganguli, Schnitzer and Jercog (2022) on CRCNS hc-30, which holds the event onsets and track positions of 110 CA1 calcium imaging sessions from 12 mice on a linear track. It rebuilds the paper's activity tensor, trial shuffle, linear SVM position decoders and signal and noise measures, and tests the effect of noise correlations on decoding accuracy, its saturation with ensemble size, the geometry of noise and signal, and the normalized signal variance.

outcomes.statement: The analysed data are 110 sessions from 12 mice with 27,898 neurons (151 to 497 per session, median 235), selected from 239 sessions for more than 150 neurons and 30 running trials in each direction; a subset of 73 sessions from 10 mice with at least 200 neurons is the large-data set.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Methods, Data preprocessing for decoding mouse position
outcomes.quote: we tracked the concurrent calcium dynamics of hundreds of CA1 pyramidal neurons in 12 mice (151-497 neurons per session, median 235; a total of 27,898 neurons over 110 sessions) ... we opted to further restrict the selection of sessions to those with at least 200 neurons. We referred to the limited subset of sessions as the “large-data” sessions (73 sessions from 10 mice)
outcomes.notes: All 110 sessions in the file meet the working rule (more than 150 neurons, more than 30 valid trials each way), from 12 mice, 27,898 neurons, median 235, 151 to 497. More than 200 neurons (code) gives 73 large-data sessions from 10 mice; 200 or more (Methods) gives 74 from 10. The file holds only the 110 working sessions, so the selection from 239 cannot be checked.
deviations: The 239 recorded sessions are not in the dataset; the 110 count is checked as the number of sessions meeting the rule, as the criterion allows.

outcomes.statement: Single-neuron responses vary strongly between visits to the same bin (response variance 0.7263 +/- 0.6117), and the single-cell signal-to-noise ratio, variance between bins over variance within bins, is 0.41 +/- 0.34, pooled over 27,898 neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Supplementary Table 1 (last column and footnote ***)
outcomes.quote: Neuronal response fluctuations were, in general, large for different visits to each spatial bin (response variance = 0.7263 + /− 0.6117, variance between bins / variance within bins = single-cell signal-to-noise ratio = 0.41 + /− 0.34, pooled from 27,898 neurons)
outcomes.notes: Code reading (SD over trials per neuron and class, pooled over 1,115,920 session, class and neuron values) 0.7263 +/- 0.6117, equal to the paper to four decimals; variance reading 0.9016 +/- 1.5301. Single-cell SNR with the 40 classes together 0.437 +/- 0.464 over 27,898 neurons (5 with no response); per direction 0.295 +/- 0.294. Both means match under the first reading; the SNR spread (0.464) is larger than the paper's 0.34.
deviations: The file holds event onsets only; the event trace is rebuilt from them with the Methods' alpha kernel (tau 0.2 s, sampled at 20 Hz from 0.05 to 1.5 s, causal) and divided by its standard deviation (Methods, Event detection algorithm, last two steps; code DecodeTensor.tensor_loader, 'HD_gamma').
All valid trials of each direction are used (code variance_per_neuron.mlx works on the session tensor), not the equalised trials of the decoder.

outcomes.statement: In these data the mean event rate is 0.33 +/- 0.24 Hz, the in-field and out-of-field rates 0.88 +/- 0.72 and 0.034 +/- 0.07 Hz, the maximum rate 1.4 +/- 0.72 Hz, the place-field width at half amplitude 37.8 +/- 48.5 cm, the trial-by-trial variability 1.2 +/- 0.66 and the spatial information 0.24 +/- 0.051 bits per event, similar to electrophysiological reports.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Table 1, row "Our Data"; Results, paragraph 1
outcomes.inferred: The values are only in Supplementary Table 1 ("Our Data" row); the Results say only that the place-field characteristics were similar to previous reports.
outcomes.notes: Two of seven values are within 10% under some reading, the mean event rate over running frames in cells with more than 100 events per 10 min (0.362 Hz) and the maximum binned rate in those cells (1.461 Hz). Out of tolerance under every reading run are the in-field rate (1.04 to 1.34 Hz against 0.88), the out-of-field rate (0.15 to 0.25 against 0.034), the fitted FWHM (16.4 to 18.5 cm against 37.8), the trial-by-trial variability (0.036 to 0.043 in event counts, 0.88 to 0.90 in the event trace, against 1.2) and the spatial information (0.15 to 0.16 by the footnote's formula read literally, 1.06 to 1.30 bits as log2(20) minus the entropy, against 0.24). The widths leave out 195 fits wider than 1180 cm (ten times the track). With no cap the mean FWHM over both directions is 37.8 cm (n 52,849), within tolerance (37.6 cm, n 52,838, in the previous run; a few Gaussian fits differ between runs), which would give three values and a partial reproduction; that mean comes from the 195 runaway fits, as the median is 11.5 cm and the mean of fits up to the track length 15.5 cm. The outcome rests on leaving those fits out. The minimal-modulation rule (maximum above 20% of the SD of the tuning curve) keeps 27,715 rightward and 27,770 leftward of 27,898 cells, against the paper's 27,793, so it is the paper's rule and removes only silent cells; it does not move the width. Gaussian fits failed for 1536 rightward and 1411 leftward tuning curves.
deviations: Readings run for the open details (criterion) are rates over running frames or the whole session; in-field within the fitted half-amplitude width or above half the peak; per-direction fits and fits pooled over both directions; all cells and cells with more than 100 events per 10 min (Supplementary Figure 3 legend). The measured values listed are, per quantity, the reading closest to the paper.

Trial-by-trial variability was computed both on event counts per visit, as the footnote says (spike count), and on the event trace tensor, a reading added because the counts are far from the paper's scale.
The footnote formula for spatial information is garbled in the text; it was read literally ((1/N) sum p log2 p, sign dropped) and as log2(N) minus the entropy of the binned rate distribution.
Assumed, Gaussian fits with a FWHM above 1180 cm (ten times the track) are fit failures and are left out of the width; the paper names no cap. Without it the mean width is within tolerance (notes).
The log2(N) minus entropy reading of spatial information assumes uniform occupancy over the 20 bins; the literal footnote formula, H/20, cannot exceed log2(20)/20 = 0.216 and so cannot reach 0.24.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlations between neuron pairs depend on the distance between their place-field peaks, highest for nearby fields, and trial shuffling drastically reduces them.
outcomes.source: Figure 1d and legend; Results, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: The shuffling procedure drastically reduced noise correlations in the shuffled data ... we found that noise correlations’ dependence on PF distance was similar to previously measured values in other brain regions
outcomes.notes: Mean over 110 sessions, rightward, distance 0 0.0386 against 0.0064 at 10 or more bins; leftward 0.0374 against 0.0058. Shuffled means at the printed distances are within 0.0002 of zero, and the 95% intervals separate from the unshuffled ones at every distance 0 to 10, in both directions; pooling all pairs gives the same. 7,859,771 pairs over both directions against the legend's 3,941,140, about half, which fits counting each pair once over the two directions.
deviations: Pairs whose correlation is undefined in a bin (a neuron silent over all trials of that bin) are averaged over the remaining bins; a pair with no defined bin is dropped.

outcomes.statement: Pairwise correlations do not depend on the physical distance between the neurons in the field of view, so they are not produced by contamination from nearby cells.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: to test if the correlations were generated through contamination from nearby cells, we confirmed that pairwise correlations were independent of the physical distance of the neurons within the recording field of view
outcomes.notes: The test needs the positions of the cells in the field of view (code neuropil_contamination_argument.m uses cell centroids, cellAnatomicLocat). event_traces.mat holds only mouse_name, session_ID, traces and position, and the data set has no other file.

outcomes.statement: Position tracking noise is small, 0.28 cm on average (0.12 to 1.0 cm across 110 sessions), far below the decoding errors.
outcomes.source: Methods, Estimate of position measurement noise; Results, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: On average, the scale of the jitter was 0.28 cm, with a range of 0.12–1.0 cm across 110 sessions

outcomes.statement: The spatial signal grows linearly with ensemble size and does not change with trial shuffling, while the noise along the signal direction keeps growing linearly in the unmodified data but saturates within about 100 neurons in the shuffled data.
outcomes.source: Figure 3c and 3d; Methods, Analyzing signal and noise in the spatial code, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: This quantity grew linearly with ensemble size and was independent of trial shuffling (Fig. 3b, c ). Similarly, we defined noise σ 2 as the trial-by-trial variance of the neuronal population responses along the signal direction between two adjacent spatial bins (Fig. 3b ). The noise in the unmodified data kept increasing linearly with ensemble size, whereas in the shuffled data, it reached saturation well within the first ~100 neurons
outcomes.notes: Shuffling leaves the bin means unchanged (largest change 7e-16), so the signal and its slope are identical with and without shuffling. Median session, unshuffled noise slope 0.0154 with R squared 0.983 at 100 neurons or more (slope positive in 110 of 110 sessions, R squared at least 0.9 in 109); shuffled noise slope 0.0012, a median 0.084 of the unshuffled slope (below 0.1 in 72 of 110 sessions).
deviations: Signal and noise use 20 random neuron subsets per ensemble size, each with its own trial split, where the paper uses 80 (Methods, Analyzing signal and noise, paragraph 3), to fit the time limit.

outcomes.statement: Along the eigenvectors of the noise covariance, each component's SNR contribution rises to a maximum at the sixth component, and the first six carry only a small part of the total, so spatial information is spread over many dimensions.
outcomes.source: Figure 4a and legend; Results, paragraph 8; Supplementary Figure 12
outcomes.quote: We found that each noise component’s contribution to the SNR increased until it reached its maximum at the sixth largest component ... The first six components only accounted for a small proportion of the neuronal ensemble’s total information
outcomes.notes: With 100 splits per bin pair as in the code, the mean over 73 sessions of the per-session median over bin pairs peaks at the 7th component (0.0730), the 6th close (0.0719). Per-session peaks have median 8; per-mouse peaks 4 to 13. The first six carry 0.358 of the sum over the 14 components that all sessions have, and a median 0.103 of each session's own sum; below one half either way.
deviations: The SNR per component uses the first h trials of each direction (h the smaller count), not a random set, and the session-mean curve is cut to the 14 components every session has. The values at components 6, 7 and 8 (0.0719, 0.0730, 0.0720) are within 1.5% of each other.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlations increase the overlap (squared cosine) between the noise principal directions and the signal direction compared with shuffled data.
outcomes.source: Figure 4b and legend; Results, paragraph 9; Supplementary Figure 15
outcomes.quote: We used the area between the two curves (gray) to quantify how noise correlations increased the overlap between the noise modes and the signal direction
outcomes.notes: All components, covariance eigenvectors, the unshuffled minus shuffled sum of cos squared is positive in 73 of 73 sessions (median 0.119) and in all 10 animal means (smallest 0.066). Up to the sixth component, median 0.137, and with correlation-matrix eigenvectors 0.200 (all) and 0.089 (six), positive in every session and animal under each reading.
deviations: The shuffle and the eigenvectors use all trials of each direction (code Cloud.m), not equalised trials.

outcomes.statement: Across animals, the increase in noise and signal overlap caused by noise correlations is inversely correlated with the asymptotic SNR (r squared 0.50, p = 0.014), so the geometry of the noise predicts where information saturates.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 4c legend
outcomes.quote: We found that the average change in total overlap between noise and signal direction was inversely correlated with the asymptotic SNR slope (i.e., Fig. 3e & Suppl. Fig. 10b ) across animals (Fig. 4c , r 2 = 0.50, p = 0.014), confirming the intuition

outcomes.statement: The RMS decoding error with all neurons is 9.38 +/- 4.06 cm with noise correlations and 5.15 +/- 2.40 cm after trial shuffling (median +/- IQR over 110 sessions), so noise correlations impair position estimates.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2d; Discussion, paragraph 8
outcomes.quote: the root mean square (RMS) error between predicted and recorded mouse positions showed that the effect of noise correlations was detrimental for position estimation across all spatial bins ... 9.38 + /−4.06 cm ... 5.15 + /−2.40 cm (median + /− IQR, n = 110 sessions)
outcomes.notes: Median RMS error over 110 sessions 9.36 cm (IQR 3.92) with correlations and 4.80 cm (IQR 1.73) shuffled; both medians and the ensemble IQR within tolerance, the shuffled IQR not. Ensemble larger in 109 of 110 sessions (Wilcoxon p = 9.0e-20). Without the six misaligned sessions 9.14 and 4.78 cm. With C = 0.1, 1 and 10 on 12 sessions the medians are 8.52, 8.86 and 8.56 cm (ensemble) and 4.98, 5.03 and 4.99 cm (shuffled). The decoder's docstring now gives C = 1, the value used; it had said 100.

The paper's unregularised fit has no exact equivalent here; C = 1 is assumed as the standard choice, and C = 0.1 and 10 are shown on 12 sessions as variants.

findings.statement: The data set holds only the 110 working sessions of the 239 recorded, and no positions of the cells in the field of view, so the paper's test that noise correlations do not depend on the distance between cells cannot be run. There is no reward or trial record; trials and task performance are rebuilt from the position.

The traces array holds event onsets (single frames with the event amplitude), as the descriptor says, not the alpha-convolved and normalised event trace the paper decodes from; the trace must be rebuilt with the Methods' kernel. Rebuilt this way, the response variability matches the paper's 0.7263 +/- 0.6117 exactly.
No sampling rate, frame times or spatial scale are stored; position is in camera pixels. 20 Hz and 118 cm over the 5th to 95th percentile of position are taken from the paper and its code.
The descriptor and the paper describe sessions of about 20 min; at 20 Hz the sessions last a median 30.1 min (20.1 to 46.0).

In six sessions the event trace does not track the position at lag 0 (a quick decoder gives 14.7 to 44.0 cm mean error, against a median 5.6 cm). In Mouse2012 141832 and Mouse2011 142436 the events lead by 80 to 90 frames (best lag error 5.4 and 2.8 cm); Mouse2011 105556 and 104511 show no position information at any lag within 200 frames; Mouse2026 115639 and Mouse2021 132808 are weaker at lag 0 (14.7 and 15.3 cm). The paper's code trims the first 350 frames of Mouse2026 115639, which suggests a known offset there. Four of them (Mouse2012 141832 and the three of Mouse2011) have flat IMSE curves and the other two low, slowly rising ones, so the IMSE fits give meaningless I0 and N: Mouse2011 105556 gives I0 = 260 with 4 subsets and 241 with 80 (against a median 1e-4), and 104511 a negative I0 and N with 4 subsets and I0 = 231 with 80.

Four sessions have negative positions (Mouse2012 141832 down to -3.7e7 pixels over 795 frames, Mouse2022 093722 down to -1.5e5 over 79 frames, Mouse2024 090858&091446 a ramp from -12,628 over the first 503 frames, and Mouse2028 105610 down to -23 over 6 frames, where the track spans about 60 to 700 pixels). The first valid trial of Mouse2022 093722 holds the 79 frames; no valid trial of the other three holds any.

Two session IDs join two recordings (Mouse2024 090858&091446 with 55,247 frames, and 130536&130559) without saying how; the first has 77.6 events per neuron per minute against a median 12.0, and its rate rises from 38.6 in the first quarter of the frames to 103.1 in the last.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebooks)
verifications.reviewed: The executed notebooks reproduce_hazon_2022.ipynb and reproduce_hazon_2022_decoding.ipynb with the conclusion cells and the summaries removed, the helper module hc30.py and the claims file, with the paper's full text. The verifier listed the CRCNS bucket hc-30/ and tested helpers on synthetic inputs (shuffle_tensor, fit_imse, jitter, select_trials). It could read only the text outputs, not the figures, and could not read the paper's MATLAB code. It had no attempt record and took the claims from the claims file.

disagreements.reason: Reproduced, resting on the code's direction. Cell 28: the legend's direction (beginning greater) gives p = 1.0. The code's direction gives p = 1.1e-18, against the code's printed 2.19e-18. The signal slope increases over the run, opposite to the claim statement.

Reproduced, resting on the confidence-interval filter. Cell 46: unfiltered, the session-level test gives p = 0.041 (<0.05, so not reproduced). With the filter Supplementary Table 2 describes, p = 0.10 for sessions and 0.077 for animals. The amplitude variance correlates across animals (r = 0.75, p = 0.013), which goes against the text's 'or amplitudes'. Problem 3: the intervals of the filter are the author's delta-method construction from slope standard errors, not the paper's method. It keeps 69 sessions where the code kept 72. The outcome depends on about 4 sessions.

NB2 cell 22: the main reading gives r = -0.07, p = 0.84, because Mouse2011's mean I0 is 23.7, set by one failed fit. Excluding failed fits and misaligned sessions gives r = 0.75, p = 0.0125: positive and p < 0.05, but not p < 0.01, and r squared = 0.56 is outside 0.73 +/- 0.073.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebooks)
verifications.reviewed: The full executed notebooks reproduce_hazon_2022.ipynb, reproduce_hazon_2022_decoding.ipynb and reproduce_hazon_2022_fitcheck.ipynb with their conclusions and summaries, the helper module hc30.py, the README, the claims file, the attempt record and the paper. It checked every Result sentence, the summaries and the notes against the printed outputs, and the round-1 points.

paper_notes.statement: The Figure 3f legend says the signal slope decreases over the run, while the code's test (signrank(begin, end, tail left)) and its printed p = 2.19e-18 test an increase; the data show an increase (medians 0.208 at the start and 0.313 at the end of runs).

The synthetic place-field model has uniform half-width distributions in the Figure 5 legend and Supplementary Figure 16, and log-normal ones in the Methods; simulated, they give opposite results for which distribution has the higher NSV.

Questions for the paper's authors. (1) Which direction does the Figure 3f signal-slope test take, the legend's decrease or the code's increase? This attempt follows the code. (2) Which half-width distributions produced Figure 5a to 5d, the legend's uniform ones or the Methods' log-normal ones? This attempt follows the legend. (3) The decoder is fitted with Lambda 0 (no regularisation); was this the setting for all published results? This attempt uses an L2 SVM with C = 1 and voting; C = 0.1 and 10 change the median error by less than 0.4 cm, and on 9 sessions loss-weighted decoding gives a median 0.71 of the fitted N. (4) How were the Supplementary Table 1 values computed (rates over running or all frames, the in-field definition, the cells averaged, the spatial information formula, and whether trial-by-trial variability uses counts or the event trace)? The readings tried give at most two of the seven values within tolerance, three if the fitted widths are not capped. (5) How were the confidence intervals of the Supplementary Table 2 filter computed? With delta-method intervals here the filter decides whether the variance of PF widths reaches p < 0.05 (0.102 with it, 0.041 without).

entries.name: hazon-2022
entries.title: Noise correlations limit hippocampal spatial accuracy (Hazon et al. 2022)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Hazon, Minces, Tomàs, Ganguli, Schnitzer and Jercog (2022) on CRCNS hc-30, which holds the event onsets and track positions of 110 CA1 calcium imaging sessions from 12 mice on a linear track. It rebuilds the paper's activity tensor, trial shuffle, linear SVM position decoders and signal and noise measures, and tests the effect of noise correlations on decoding accuracy, its saturation with ensemble size, the geometry of noise and signal, and the normalized signal variance.
